title: News consumption is moving toward social video and personality-led platforms while trust and verification remain contested
source_unit: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, Digital News Report 2025
geography: 48 markets across six continents, with specific United States and cross-market comparisons

denominator.unit: markets covered by the Digital News Report 2025 online-news-consumer study

social_video_news.unit: percent of the global sample consuming social-video news in 2025, up from 52% in 2020

any_video_news.unit: percent consuming any online news video in 2025, up from 67% in 2020

platform_fragmentation.value: six online networks now reach more than 10% weekly with news, compared with two a decade ago

observations.method: Reuters Institute comparative survey analysis across 48 markets, with longitudinal comparisons of digital news use and platform reach; the record uses published aggregate estimates rather than respondent-level files.
observations.uncertainty: Online samples are not nationally representative in every market and platform-use questions measure reported exposure, not attention quality, comprehension, persuasion, or causal political behavior. Platform algorithms and definitions change over time.
observations.subgroup: Online news users by market, age, platform, format preference, political orientation, and relationship to legacy media and creators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Video and social platforms can widen access, support local or niche voices, and complement rather than replace trusted publishers; increased reach does not automatically mean lower-quality information.

observations.period: 2025; United States news-source and personality ecosystem

denominator.unit: United States online-news-consumer comparison frame in the Digital News Report

social_video_news_us.unit: percent accessing news via social media and video networks in the United States, versus 50% TV news and 48% news websites/apps

young_adult_social_video_main_source.value: 54% of 18-24s and 50% of 25-34s in the US say social/video networks are their main news source

creator_exposure.unit: percent of the US sample encountering Joe Rogan discussing or commenting on news in the prior week

observations.method: Reuters Institute country analysis using the 2025 comparative online-news-consumer survey and platform/source questions.
observations.uncertainty: The figures describe reported exposure and main-source designation, not endorsement, persuasion, or voting. The US field period and political context may affect estimates, and named-person exposure does not establish influence.
observations.subgroup: US online news users by age, political orientation, gender, trust in mainstream media, and platform or personality exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Personality-led media may reach audiences traditional outlets do not, and users can combine creators with trusted news brands, official sources, and fact-checkers rather than substituting one for another.

observations.period: 2025; online news trust, verification, and AI mediation

denominator.unit: markets in the Digital News Report comparative trust and misinformation frame

concern_real_vs_false.unit: percent expressing concern about telling what is true from false online news

weekly_ai_news_use.unit: percent using AI chatbots for news in a typical week overall, rising to 15% among under-25s

overall_news_trust.unit: percent saying they trust most news most of the time; stable for the third consecutive year

verification_routes.value: trusted news outlets 38%, official sources 35%, fact-checkers 25%, and social media 14% as first routes to check suspected false information

observations.method: Reuters Institute aggregate cross-market survey analysis of trust, misinformation concerns, verification behavior, AI news use, and attitudes toward platform moderation and personalization.
observations.uncertainty: Concern about misinformation may partly reflect disagreement or perceived bias rather than objectively false content. Reported verification intentions are not verified behavior, and trust is not accuracy or institutional legitimacy.
observations.subgroup: Online news users by age, market, political orientation, news-literacy training, platform use, and trust in news, official institutions, influencers, and AI systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable aggregate trust can coexist with severe country and group differences; AI summaries may improve accessibility while reducing transparency or perceived accuracy, and social verification can supplement rather than displace formal sources.

related_sources.claim: Reuters Institute publication and methodology announcement for the 48-market report.
Digital News Report 2025 navigation and chapter materials.

boundary: This record adds a cross-market news-platform, trust, creator, and AI-mediation route. It is based on published aggregate survey estimates, not a local respondent-level analysis; it does not establish individual persuasion, voting effects, misinformation exposure, creator influence, platform causality, or institutional legitimacy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Reuters Institute executive summary and publication page were retrieved; market scope, social-video trend, US platform shares, trust, verification, AI-use, and uncertainty notes were cross-checked against the official report pages. The hash is a source-URL fingerprint for the executive-summary page.
